name: THE SOMEONE RACLETTE THE BED BURGER (comes with raclette cheese)

recipe.history:
Raclette is both a cheese and a cooking tradition from the Alpine regions of Switzerland and the Savoie and Haute-Savoie departments of eastern France — a place where the mountains dictate everything about the way people eat, work, and gather. The word 'raclette' comes from the French verb racler, meaning to scrape, which describes the centuries-old technique of holding a half-wheel of cheese near an open fire, heat source, or purpose-built grill until the cut face softens and bubbles, then scraping the molten layer directly onto a plate of boiled potatoes, cured meats, and cornichons. The cheese itself is a semi-firm, washed-rind variety made from cow's milk, with a pale straw interior, a pungent, slightly funky orange rind, and a flavor that is simultaneously buttery, nutty, and earthy with a tang that deepens under heat. Historical records of raclette-style eating in the Swiss Alps date to the medieval period, when shepherds and farmers in the mountains would heat cheese near campfires during long winters. The modern raclette machine — an electric device with small individual trays heated from below, around which friends gather to melt their own portions — transformed the dish from alpine necessity into one of the great social rituals of Swiss and French culture.

Raclette arrived in the United States primarily through the specialty cheese and fondue craze of the 1970s and then gained renewed visibility in the 2010s as cheese culture exploded on social media — videos of molten raclette being scraped dramatically over food went viral repeatedly, turning an ancient Alpine tradition into a contemporary visual phenomenon. American restaurants and food halls began offering raclette boards and raclette-topped dishes, and creative chefs quickly recognized that a cheese with such extreme meltability and distinctive flavor deserved a place on a burger. Raclette on a burger is a revelation: it melts into a smooth, glossy, almost elastic blanket of cheese, and its slightly pungent, nutty flavor stands up to the savory power of a seared beef patty without being overwhelmed. The Alpine tradition of serving it with cornichons and cured meat translates almost perfectly to classic burger accompaniments.

The first time I made raclette at home I owned neither a raclette machine nor a fireplace, so I improvised by placing thick slices of raclette on a cast-iron skillet over medium heat and watching them melt into translucent, bubbling sheets that I then draping over food like warm blankets. The effect was similar, if less theatrical than the traditional scraping — the cheese was molten and flowing, intensely aromatic, and it coated everything it touched with a smooth, nutty richness that lingered in a very satisfying way. When I put it over a burger patty, the combination of the Maillard-crusted beef and the flowing, funky cheese felt genuinely Alpine — substantial, warming, designed for people who had been outdoors in cold air and needed something that would anchor them completely. I have been grateful for that improvised discovery many times since.

Medium rare is the cooking specification for this patty: 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, or 54 to 57 degrees Celsius on an instant-read thermometer, followed by a three-minute rest. This is not simply preference — it is the requirement of the cheese. Raclette's entire appeal is its meltability, the way it flows and coats and becomes almost liquid with heat. For that flow to mean anything, it needs something to flow over that is still yielding, still moist, still releasing the juices that a medium-rare patty holds. An overcooked patty is a closed surface — the cheese pools on top and slides off. A medium-rare patty is an open one — the cheese sinks slightly into the crust's pores and mingles with the juices and the two become a single, extraordinary thing. Cook it right. Raclette deserves it.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
8 oz raclette cheese, rind removed, cut into 1/4-inch slices
4 oz thinly sliced dry-cured ham (jambon cru, or prosciutto as substitute)
Salt and white pepper to taste
For the boiled fingerling potatoes (side/topping option):
instructions: 1. Boil the fingerling potatoes: Place potatoes in a pot of cold water with 1 tbsp salt. Bring to a boil and cook 15–18 minutes until tender when pierced with a knife. Drain, toss with butter and chives, season with salt and pepper. Keep warm. These can be served alongside or sliced and placed inside the burger.

2. Make the Dijon-herb aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, Dijon mustard, whole grain mustard, parsley, chives, grated garlic, and white wine vinegar. Season with salt and white pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

3. Make the bun dough: Combine yeast, sugar, and warm milk in a stand mixer bowl. Let bloom 5 minutes. Add egg, butter, salt, and flour. Mix with dough hook on medium speed 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

4. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 balls, shape into bun rounds on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with caraway seeds if using. Bake 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool completely.
5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into patties 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple. Season both sides with salt, black pepper, and white pepper.

6. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties undisturbed 3 minutes. Flip and immediately drape 2–3 slices of raclette over each patty. Cover the skillet with a lid or domed heat-proof bowl to trap steam and help the cheese melt. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The raclette should be fully melted and flowing over the edges. Rest 3 minutes.
7. Toast bun halves cut-side down in the skillet 60 seconds.

8. Assemble: Spread Dijon-herb aioli generously on both bun halves. Place arugula tossed lightly with olive oil on the bottom bun. Add the medium-rare, raclette-draped patty. Layer sliced dry-cured ham over the cheese. Arrange cornichon slices across the top. Optionally, add 2–3 sliced fingerling potatoes inside the burger for a true Alpine experience. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve immediately with remaining fingerling potatoes on the side.
